vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: to point out a problem early, so that somebody else can act on it
failing to take the care that any reasonable person in that job would have taken
to take a problem to somebody more senior, because it is bigger than you
something important that was missed by accident, not by decision
knowing the risk perfectly well and going ahead anyway
the checking a careful professional does before signing or agreeing to anything
a rule or a step put in place to stop a risk somebody already knew about
expected to explain and answer for a decision you made, in front of other people

paras: On the fourteenth of February a trainee read a draft agreement and noticed that clause nine and clause fourteen said opposite things about who carried the cost of a delay. Two clauses in conflict is a red flag in any contract, in any language, and she was right about it. She wrote one sentence about it at the bottom of a longer email, sent to four people, none of whom replied. Two days later the supervising partner signed off on the draft. Eight months after that, a delay happened, the two clauses met each other in a client's accounts department, and the file was reopened.

The panel that reads the file now has a narrow question and a wide one. The narrow one is whether the four recipients saw the email. They must have seen it, because it went to four people and three of them were in the office all week; one of them cannot have read it, because she was on leave from the twelfth. The wide question is harder. The firm has a safeguard for exactly this situation: any draft with a flagged inconsistency needs a second read before sign-off. Nobody switched that safeguard off. It simply did not run, because the flag was one line at the bottom of an email about something else, and a safeguard that depends on somebody noticing a sentence is not a safeguard at all.

So the panel has to choose between three words, and the three words carry very different consequences. An oversight is something missed by accident. A lapse is a short failure in somebody who is usually careful. Negligence is failing to take the care that a reasonable person in that job would have taken, and the test is not what this person did but what a reasonable one would have done. The trainee did the hardest part, which is noticing. She should have escalated it, and she should have said it twice, once in writing and once out loud to one named person. She need not have worried about looking foolish: nobody in that firm would have remembered a question that turned out to be nothing.

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: She should have escalated it to one named person, out loud.
The firm should not have signed off on it without a second read.
They must have seen the email. It went to four people.
She cannot have read it. It arrived after she left.
Somebody might have caught it, but nobody was looking.
She needn't have worried about looking foolish.

listenings.text: People come to these panels expecting a moral question, and it is not one. There is a test, and the test is boring: what would a reasonable person in the same job, on the same afternoon, with the same workload, have done. If a reasonable person would have caught it, the word stops being oversight and starts being something else, and everybody in the room can feel the temperature change when that happens. Now, about the trainee. She did the hardest part, and I want that written down. Noticing is the hard part. Anybody can act on a problem once four partners agree it exists. What she should have done was escalate it, properly, to one person by name, and I will say in her defence that at twenty-four almost nobody does, because escalating feels like accusing four senior people of not reading their own email. The thing panels almost always get wrong is that they go looking for the person instead of the safeguard. We had a safeguard. A flagged inconsistency needs a second read before sign-off. It did not run. Nobody switched it off, so somebody, at some point, must have decided quietly that the second read was optional, and that decision is older than this file and bigger than anybody in this room.

It was one line, at the bottom of an email about three other things. And I want to be honest about why I wrote it that way, because for a long time I told myself it was because I was busy. It was not. I wrote it small on purpose. If I was wrong about the clauses, a small sentence at the bottom of a long email could be missed, and nobody would remember that I had made four senior people stop and check something for nothing. That was the fear. Not being wrong about the contract. I was fairly sure about the contract. The fear was being the person who wasted everybody's afternoon and then turned out to have misread it. Two years on, I know how ridiculous that sounds, and I also know that everybody I trained with did exactly the same thing. What do I do now? I say it twice. Once in writing, and once out loud to one person by name, and I finish with a sentence I stole from somebody more senior than me: tell me if this is nothing. It gives the other person somewhere easy to go, and it means the thing has been said in a room, out loud, where an email cannot be scrolled past.
